account: Rainforest Connection (RFCx), a US non-profit founded by Topher White, deploys solar-powered “Guardian” acoustic sensors. In its own words, they use “sound & artificial intelligence” to track chainsaws, vehicle engines, hunting dogs and gunshots. They send real-time alerts to a mobile app so that “an agent nearby” can respond. RFCx states it has protected over 726,000 (impact page) or 750,000 (guardian page) hectares across 8,662+ projects in 137 countries. The only non-vendor account read is a Thomson Reuters Foundation report published by The Straits Times on 11 February 2021. It is from Solok regency, West Sumatra, Indonesia, where 27 Guardian sensors had been installed more than a year earlier. Audio streams are analyzed by AI trained to pick out chainsaw sounds, and an alert goes to community patrols. Patroller Jasrialdi said logging “has totally stopped” in the area. The head of West Sumatra's forestry department, Yozarwardi Usama Putra, said he would like to expand the “early-warning system”. The same report attributes the decline in logging to a wider enforcement crackdown as well. It says RFCx planned to collect data for peer review to prove the system curbs logging. No park authority, ministry or court document records a specific alert leading to an interception, so no event is recorded.

ai_role.statement: RFCx's own pages describe AI classification of streamed audio generating app alerts for responders. The 2021 Reuters report confirms the mechanism at the Solok site: AI picks out chainsaw sounds and patrols are alerted. It quotes a patroller that logging stopped, while also crediting a government enforcement crackdown. Apart from that single news item, only the maker's account is among the sources. No park authority, ministry or court record of an AI-triggered interception was found. RFCx itself said in 2021 that peer-review data to prove the effect was still being collected.

fields.account: Rainforest Connection (RFCx), a US non-profit founded by Topher White, deploys solar-powered “Guardian” acoustic sensors. In its own words, they use “sound & artificial intelligence” to track chainsaws, vehicle engines, hunting dogs and gunshots. They send real-time alerts to a mobile app so that “an agent nearby” can respond. RFCx states it has protected over 726,000 (impact page) or 750,000 (guardian page) hectares across 8,662+ projects in 137 countries. The only non-vendor account read is a Thomson Reuters Foundation report published by The Straits Times on 11 February 2021. It is from Solok regency, West Sumatra, Indonesia, where 27 Guardian sensors had been installed more than a year earlier. Audio streams are analyzed by AI trained to pick out chainsaw sounds, and an alert goes to community patrols. Patroller Jasrialdi said logging “has totally stopped” in the area. The head of West Sumatra's forestry department, Yozarwardi Usama Putra, said he would like to expand the “early-warning system”. The same report attributes the decline in logging to a wider enforcement crackdown as well. It says RFCx planned to collect data for peer review to prove the system curbs logging. No park authority, ministry or court document records a specific alert leading to an interception, so no event is recorded.
